scenes.tts: How can rain falling on a farm help build a crab in the Chesapeake Bay? Keep your eyes on one watershed, where land, river, and Bay stay connected.
scenes.caption: How can rain falling on a farm help build a crab in the Chesapeake Bay? Keep your eyes on one watershed, where land, river, and Bay stay connected.
scenes.visual: Hook before title. Fill the frame with one continuous schematic cross-section: farm at left, winding river center, Chesapeake Bay at right, sky above. Rain sweeps from cloud to field, then blue droplets run toward the river. A crab silhouette rises in the Bay beside a large question mark. Label the whole picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: How can rain falling on a farm help build a crab in the Chesapeake Bay? Keep your eyes on one watershed, where land, river, and Bay stay connected.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the same dimmed watershed. Keep the river visibly flowing behind the title.

scenes.tts: Blue will track water, orange will track carbon, and green will track nitrogen. Each colored token can pause in a reservoir. A reservoir is a place where matter can stay, such as air, water, soil, or a living thing.
scenes.caption: Blue will track water, orange will track carbon, and green will track nitrogen. Each colored token can pause in a reservoir. A reservoir is a place where matter can stay, such as air, water, soil, or a living thing.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP: water blue, carbon orange, nitrogen green, sunlight gold, human-added flow red outline only. Keep this map for both films. Place large labeled reservoir regions directly in the carried landscape: AIR, SOIL, RIVER AND BAY, LIVING THINGS. Blue, orange, and green tokens drift slowly within their regions.
scenes.narration: Blue will track water, orange will track carbon, and green will track nitrogen. Each colored token can pause in a reservoir. A reservoir is a place where matter can stay, such as air, water, soil, or a living thing.

scenes.tts: Start with orange carbon dioxide in air and water. Algae and plants use photosynthesis to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Food moves that carbon through living things, until some reaches the crab.
scenes.caption: Start with orange carbon dioxide in air and water. Algae and plants use photosynthesis to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Food moves that carbon through living things, until some reaches the crab.
scenes.visual: Orange tokens drift in air and Bay. Gold sunlight reaches a plant and algae. On 'photosynthesis', orange tokens transform into orange SUGAR blocks inside them. Carry one block along a thick food arrow through a small animal into the crab. Keep all arrows within the same landscape.
scenes.narration: Start with orange carbon dioxide in air and water. Algae and plants use photosynthesis to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Food moves that carbon through living things, until some reaches the crab.

scenes.tts: The crab's cells use respiration, releasing carbon dioxide to the water. Plants and microbes respire too. When organisms die, decomposers break down their bodies. Microbial respiration returns much of their carbon to air or water.
scenes.caption: The crab's cells use respiration, releasing carbon dioxide to the water. Plants and microbes respire too. When organisms die, decomposers break down their bodies. Microbial respiration returns much of their carbon to air or water.
scenes.visual: The orange block inside the crab splits into several orange carbon-dioxide tokens that drift into the Bay. Repeat smaller outward motions from plant and microbe cartoons. A fallen leaf sinks into soil, gains a DECOMPOSERS label, and releases orange tokens upward and into water.
scenes.narration: The crab's cells use respiration, releasing carbon dioxide to the water. Plants and microbes respire too. When organisms die, decomposers break down their bodies. Microbial respiration returns much of their carbon to air or water.

scenes.tts: Water has its own route through evaporation, clouds, precipitation, and flow across land. It also carries other matter. Blue runoff can pick up green nitrogen from a field and move it into a river.
scenes.caption: Water has its own route through evaporation, clouds, precipitation, and flow across land. It also carries other matter. Blue runoff can pick up green nitrogen from a field and move it into a river.
scenes.visual: Blue Bay water rises as vapor, condenses into the existing cloud, falls as rain, and streams across the field. Green nitrogen tokens wait in soil. Blue runoff encloses several green tokens and carries them into the river without recoloring them.
scenes.narration: Water has its own route through evaporation, clouds, precipitation, and flow across land. It also carries other matter. Blue runoff can pick up green nitrogen from a field and move it into a river.

scenes.tts: Most organisms cannot use nitrogen gas directly. Certain microbes convert it into ammonia, and other microbes help make nitrate. Plants and algae take up ammonium or nitrate. Food can then carry that nitrogen to the crab.
scenes.caption: Most organisms cannot use nitrogen gas directly. Certain microbes convert it into ammonia, and other microbes help make nitrate. Plants and algae take up ammonium or nitrate. Food can then carry that nitrogen to the crab.
scenes.visual: Green NITROGEN GAS tokens in air approach a plant but stop. Zoom within the same field to large microbe cartoons in soil and a root nodule. Tokens change labels in order: NITROGEN GAS to AMMONIA, then NITRATE. A plant takes in a green token, which follows the carried food arrow toward the crab.
scenes.narration: Most organisms cannot use nitrogen gas directly. Certain microbes convert it into ammonia, and other microbes help make nitrate. Plants and algae take up ammonium or nitrate. Food can then carry that nitrogen to the crab.

scenes.tts: Waste and dead bodies keep nitrogen moving. Decomposers return their nitrogen to ammonium. In wet soil or mud with little oxygen, bacteria can change nitrate back into nitrogen gas. That gas returns to the air.
scenes.caption: Waste and dead bodies keep nitrogen moving. Decomposers return their nitrogen to ammonium. In wet soil or mud with little oxygen, bacteria can change nitrate back into nitrogen gas. That gas returns to the air.
scenes.visual: Carry a green token from waste and a dead leaf to decomposer cartoons, then relabel it AMMONIUM and leave it in soil. Separately, carry a green NITRATE token from the earlier nitrification step into a large wet-mud patch labeled LOW OXYGEN. A denitrifying bacteria cartoon changes NITRATE to NITROGEN GAS, and that token rises into air. Never turn the AMMONIUM token into gas.
scenes.narration: Waste and dead bodies keep nitrogen moving. Decomposers return their nitrogen to ammonium. In wet soil or mud with little oxygen, bacteria can change nitrate back into nitrogen gas. That gas returns to the air.

scenes.tts: Now follow an orange carbon token inside the crab. When the crab respires, which reservoir receives that carbon next? Hold your answer while the token waits.
scenes.caption: Now follow an orange carbon token inside the crab. When the crab respires, which reservoir receives that carbon next? Hold your answer while the token waits.
scenes.visual: Zoom back to the Bay. Enlarge one orange token inside the crab. Show three large possible destinations around it: AIR, WATER, and SOIL. Keep the question at the top and make the token pulse gently. Do not reveal an answer.
scenes.narration: Now follow an orange carbon token inside the crab. When the crab respires, which reservoir receives that carbon next? Hold your answer while the token waits.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the three possible reservoirs and question visible. The orange token pulses slowly; Bay water continues a gentle wave motion.

scenes.tts: The surrounding water receives carbon dioxide from the crab's respiration. That carbon may later enter algae, leave the water, or travel elsewhere. A cycle is a network of possible routes, not one track every atom repeats.
scenes.caption: The surrounding water receives carbon dioxide from the crab's respiration. That carbon may later enter algae, leave the water, or travel elsewhere. A cycle is a network of possible routes, not one track every atom repeats.
scenes.visual: Highlight WATER, then move the orange token from crab into the Bay as a CARBON DIOXIDE block. From that block, grow several thin dotted arrows toward algae, surface air, and downstream water. Mark every route 'possible' and keep the whole network labeled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The surrounding water receives carbon dioxide from the crab's respiration. That carbon may later enter algae, leave the water, or travel elsewhere. A cycle is a network of possible routes, not one track every atom repeats.

scenes.tts: Notice how the paths share the same world. Blue water carries green nitrogen. Algae can hold orange carbon and green nitrogen together. Animals receive both through food, while decomposers send both onward again.
scenes.caption: Notice how the paths share the same world. Blue water carries green nitrogen. Algae can hold orange carbon and green nitrogen together. Animals receive both through food, while decomposers send both onward again.
scenes.visual: Restore the full watershed. Trace the blue runoff with green passengers, then highlight one alga containing separate orange and green blocks. Both colors travel together along a food arrow to the crab. After a small dead-organism icon appears, decomposer cartoons move both colors to new reservoirs.
scenes.narration: Notice how the paths share the same world. Blue water carries green nitrogen. Algae can hold orange carbon and green nitrogen together. Animals receive both through food, while decomposers send both onward again.

scenes.tts: At the Bay's surface, orange carbon dioxide can dissolve into seawater. Carbon dioxide also comes back out. Ocean absorption names one direction in a two-way exchange between air and water.
scenes.caption: At the Bay's surface, orange carbon dioxide can dissolve into seawater. Carbon dioxide also comes back out. Ocean absorption names one direction in a two-way exchange between air and water.
scenes.visual: Zoom to the air-water boundary. Move orange carbon-dioxide tokens both downward into the Bay and upward into air using two separate arrows. Keep both arrows active, alternate their widths slowly, and label the exchange 'direction can change'.
scenes.narration: At the Bay's surface, orange carbon dioxide can dissolve into seawater. Carbon dioxide also comes back out. Ocean absorption names one direction in a two-way exchange between air and water.

scenes.tts: In ecosystems, atoms move between reservoirs, and processes connect their cycles. The crab is not an endpoint. It is one temporary reservoir in a moving watershed of air, land, water, microbes, and food.
scenes.caption: In ecosystems, atoms move between reservoirs, and processes connect their cycles. The crab is not an endpoint. It is one temporary reservoir in a moving watershed of air, land, water, microbes, and food.
scenes.visual: Draw a large loop around the carried watershed, then replace it with several intersecting arrows to avoid implying one fixed circle. Orange, green, and blue tokens keep moving through different reservoirs. Settle on the crab as one highlighted reservoir, then zoom out to the full connected scene.
scenes.narration: In ecosystems, atoms move between reservoirs, and processes connect their cycles. The crab is not an endpoint. It is one temporary reservoir in a moving watershed of air, land, water, microbes, and food.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only over a darkened, slowly moving watershed: 'In ecosystems, atoms move between reservoirs, and processes connect their cycles.'
